inline_comments.comment: `getGitDir()` unconditionally returns `join(root, '.git')`, which is wrong for git linked worktrees. In a linked worktree, `.git` is a regular text file whose contents are `gitdir: /path/to/main/.git/worktrees/<name>`. The downstream `watchFile` calls then target non-existent paths (`<worktree>/.git/HEAD`, etc.), fail with ENOENT, and are silently swallowed — leaving linked-worktree users with no git-state change detection and no feedback. The implementation needs to `stat` the `.git` path: if it is a file, read its `gitdir:` pointer and use that resolved path instead. (The current repo already has this fix — `stat` the path, fall back to the pointer if it is a file.)

`void this.configureBranchWatcher(gitDir)` discards the returned promise with no error handling, but `configureBranchWatcher` can reject: `readHeadRef` re-throws any error whose `code` is not `'ENOENT'` (e.g., `EACCES` on a permission-denied read of `.git/HEAD`). The rejection will surface as an `UnhandledPromiseRejection` and crash Node.js in strict-mode environments. Either chain `.catch(() => { /* opportunistic */ })` here, or have `readHeadRef` swallow all errors and return `undefined`. The resolved implementation uses `void this.configureBranchWatcher(gitDir).catch(() => { ... })` with a `logger.warn`.

Watching individual file paths (`.git/HEAD`, `.git/packed-refs`, `refs/heads/main`) is unreliable on Linux. Node.js `fs.watch` on Linux uses inotify, which watches inodes, not paths. Git writes ref files atomically: it writes to a temp file and `rename(2)`s it over the target, creating a new inode. After the first commit, inotify is tracking the old inode — the watcher receives an initial event and then goes silent for all subsequent commits on the same branch. Watching the parent directory (e.g., `.git/` for HEAD/packed-refs, `refs/heads/` for branch refs) catches `IN_MOVED_TO` reliably regardless of atomic replacement. The updated implementation in the repo switches to directory-level watching for exactly this reason.

The `GitFileSystem` interface only includes `watch` and `readFile`, which makes it impossible to test or inject the `stat` call needed to detect whether `.git` is a directory or a gitdir-pointer file (required for worktree support). The resolved file adds `stat: typeof stat` to this interface and the mock. Since the worktree fix is the logical follow-on to this PR, adding `stat` here would keep the interface extensible and avoid a future breaking change to the injection API.

`void callback` is an unusual way to suppress an "unused variable" warning. The `void` operator evaluates its operand and discards the result, but this pattern is non-idiomatic and easy to misread as intentional side-effect code. Use the standard TypeScript convention of a leading underscore: rename the parameter to `_callback`. This communicates the intent clearly without the operator ceremony.

`headReads.shift() ?? headReads[0] ?? 'ref: refs/heads/main
'` does not achieve its apparent intent of "return the last value repeatedly once the array is exhausted". `shift()` removes and returns the last element; after that, `headReads` is empty, so `headReads[0]` is also `undefined`, and the constant fallback activates. Any test that relies on the "repeat last" semantic will silently use `'ref: refs/heads/main
'` instead. To repeat the last value, peek before shifting: `headReads[1] != null ? headReads.shift()! : headReads[0] ?? 'ref: refs/heads/main
'`, or use a different structure (e.g., always pop and keep the last in a separate variable).

general_comments.comment: The `watcher.on('error', ...)` handler in `watchFile` removes only the single failing watcher from `this.watchers` and then returns silently. After a watcher error, the remaining watchers (HEAD, packed-refs, or branch) stay active but the system is now in a partially-functioning state — for example, if the HEAD watcher fails, branch-switch events are no longer detected, but packed-refs changes still fire. There is no log message to alert the user that monitoring has degraded. The evolved implementation takes the opposite approach: any watcher error calls `stopWatching()` (tears everything down) and emits a `logger.warn`, trading partial coverage for a clear, recoverable failure signal.

The new `GitDiffProvider` tests cover subscription, unsubscription, HEAD-change reconfiguration, and shared-watcher reuse, which is a solid set. However, no test exercises the `watcher.on('error', ...)` path added in `watchFile`. Firing an error on one of the mock watchers and asserting that the watcher is closed and removed from `this.watchers` (but the remaining watchers are unaffected) would make the error-recovery contract explicit and guard against regressions.
